summary.title: Threat Modeling | OWASP Foundation
summary.one_liner: Threat modeling is a continuous, structured process for identifying threats to a system, choosing countermeasures, and checking the results, guided by OWASP's four-question framework.
takeaways: A threat model is a structured view of an application and its environment through a security lens, including assumptions, potential threats, mitigations, and validation.
Use the four-question framework: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good job?
Threat modeling should be applied continuously across the lifecycle and updated after new features, security incidents, or architectural changes.
Techniques such as STRIDE, kill chains, and attack trees can help identify what can go wrong; a brainstorm can also work.
A good threat model produces a prioritized list of security improvements and an assurance argument that justifies the system's security.
summary.summary: This OWASP community page introduces threat modeling as a family of activities for finding threats and defining countermeasures for software, systems, and business processes. It explains what a threat model contains and why it should be refined throughout the development lifecycle rather than done once. The page organizes the work around a four-question framework and names methods such as STRIDE, kill chains, and attack trees. It also mentions the 2020 Threat Modeling Manifesto and the benefits of producing an assurance argument.
